newsitem.title: MEXICO: Banco de Mexico defends shift to repos as key tool.
newsitem.headline: Banco de Mexico defends shift to repos as key tool.

text.p: A shift in the way Banco de Mexico handles liquidity in the money markets does not represent a change in monetary policy, a central bank spokesman said on Monday.
Instead of deposit auctions, the central bank last week began to use repurchase agreements (repos) of Cetes, or treasury bills, as its main tool to drain liquidity from the money markets.
Banco de Mexico also raised the limits on the balances commercial banks could have with the central bank. Officials said both moves could be considered temporary.
"We have not changed the goal of our monetary policy. It is only an operational modification," Banco de Mexico spokesman Eduardo Turrent said about the new repo operations.

While some analysts said the move to repos was a signal the central bank wanted to promote lower short-term rates, the central bank said the shift was made for practical reasons and it allowed commercial banks to receive negotiable paper.
Banco de Mexico's official policy is that it aims to meet demand for liquidity and does not have any interest rate or exchange rate targets.
Central bank watchers said the shifts were brought about by a liquidity squeeze that became particularly intense last week.

"The concentration of excess liquidity in a few banks had been pushing rates up, a problem that the use of the more liquid Cetes should diminish," said J.P. Morgan analyst Lara Christianson, in a report released on Monday.
She said the shift has eliminated the spread between the central bank deposit rates and Cetes interest rates.
Markets had also sometimes incorrectly read the rate spread as a signal for policy changes, analysts said.
"Changes in this rate spread had been perceived as a signal of policy tightening or easing, when in fact policy was unchanged," Christianson said.

Analysts said the use of repos for daily open market operations would help banks finance the loans they made to the central bank. The switch to repos allows the central bank to provide collateral for the loans its receives.
The move could create more competition among commercial banks that lend to the central bank and indirectly allow rates to fall, analysts said.
Moreover, they said the central bank was reducing its borrowing costs and smoothing its maturity profile by offering different Cetes maturities.
The central bank has also been selling Cetes directly into the market.
Moreover, Banco de Mexico has raised the limits on the accumulated balance that commercial banks can carry with the central bank without penalties.
That move should should help the central bank reach its monetary objectives -- of keeping to a neutral stance -- without driving up interest rates, analysts said.

Heavy dollar inflows into Mexico -- from the state oil company Pemex, public sector bonds and the central bank's dollar purchase scheme -- have made it more difficult for the central bank to meet its objective of containing growth of the country's monetary base, analysts said.
